headline: High: OpenMetadata’s MCP/API surfaces and ms-swift’s shell/filesystem access create default-path risks for prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: OpenMetadata exposes MCP server, APIs, events, and webhooks, while ms-swift reads stdin/stdout and files and can execute shell commands. That creates a plausible default bridge where attacker-controlled metadata or webhook content can be treated as instructions by ms-swift. The interaction is inferred, not directly evidenced, so uncertainty pushes severity upward.
conditions: IF OpenMetadata webhook or MCP payloads are forwarded into ms-swift prompts or stdin/stdout without sanitization, injection is possible.
IF ms-swift parses catalog text or event payloads as instructions, attacker-controlled content can steer tool use.
mitigations: Disable direct prompting from webhook/MCP payloads.
Add a fixed delimiter and allowlist for fields copied between agents.
Require human review before ms-swift executes shell commands from external text.
Log and flag any instruction-like tokens in OpenMetadata outputs.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between OpenMetadata and ms-swift.

B_data_leakage.rationale: ms-swift touches datasets, checkpoints, logs, configuration, and secrets such as hub_token/sdk-token, while OpenMetadata handles governance, lineage, and memory/tribal knowledge through APIs, SDKs, events, and webhooks. A shared workspace or copied outputs could leak sensitive operational data into OpenMetadata records or downstream integrations. No direct shared filesystem is documented, so this remains a default-path but inferred risk.
conditions: IF ms-swift logs or exports checkpoints/configuration containing secrets into OpenMetadata-managed metadata, leakage occurs.
IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or event stream, sensitive files can be ingested into OpenMetadata outputs.
mitigations: Exclude secrets and tokens from ms-swift logs.
Restrict OpenMetadata ingestion to approved metadata fields only.
Rotate any hub_token/sdk-token exposed in shared outputs.
Review one sample event for accidental file-content capture.
requires-engineering: enforce field-level redaction in the integration.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ms-swift can write the filesystem, execute shell, install packages, and spawn subprocesses; OpenMetadata is runnable and uses MCP tools, APIs, SDKs, events, and webhooks. If both are attached to the same mutable workspace or service account, they can contend over shared files or metadata state. The profiles do not state locking or isolation, so the conflict pathway is plausible and not blocked.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or config store, last-writer-wins conflicts can occur.
IF OpenMetadata webhooks trigger ms-swift jobs concurrently, shared artifacts may be overwritten.
mitigations: Separate working directories per agent.
Serialize writes with a simple lock file.
Disable concurrent webhook-triggered jobs for the shared target.
Check for overlapping filenames before execution.
requires-engineering: add transactional coordination for shared resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: OpenMetadata’s governance and lineage outputs can become authoritative context for ms-swift, and ms-swift can then act via shell or file writes. If OpenMetadata emits incorrect metadata or lineage, ms-swift may propagate it into downstream artifacts without verification. Because the pair lacks a documented verification gate and both agents can act on outputs, the blast radius can extend beyond a single work product.
conditions: IF ms-swift consumes OpenMetadata lineage or governance fields as authoritative input, errors can cascade into generated outputs.
IF ms-swift uses OpenMetadata-derived facts to write files or run shell actions, downstream mistakes become persistent.
mitigations: Require a verification step before ms-swift acts on OpenMetadata data.
Compare OpenMetadata facts against a second source for critical fields.
Mark generated metadata as untrusted until reviewed.
Limit ms-swift actions to dry-run mode for one test cycle.
requires-engineering: add confidence thresholds before downstream actions.

E_compliance.rationale: ms-swift explicitly handles hub_token and sdk-token plus datasets, checkpoints, and logs, while OpenMetadata stores governance, lineage, and memory/tribal knowledge through APIs and webhooks. If regulated or sensitive data is cataloged, the pair can create retention and subject-rights mismatches between operational files and metadata records. The profiles do not specify residency or certifications, so I cannot justify high severity.
conditions: IF regulated data is cataloged in OpenMetadata while ms-swift retains logs or checkpoints longer than policy allows, retention mismatch occurs.
IF deletion requests are applied to OpenMetadata but not to ms-swift artifacts, subject-rights handling is incomplete.
mitigations: Inventory which data classes flow through both agents.
Set a short retention window for ms-swift logs and checkpoints.
Document deletion/export steps for both systems.
Exclude regulated fields from OpenMetadata ingestion.
requires-engineering: align residency and retention controls across both tools.
